units.name: application-core
units.role: The Flask application object: URL routing table, WSGI dispatch, and the hook/decorator system.
units.description: This is the heart of Flask: the application object a developer creates at the start of every project (app = Flask(__name__)). It holds the table of URL routes and decides which Python function should run for each incoming web request. It manages the hooks developers can register to run code before a request, after a request, or when an error occurs, and provides the decorator methods (route, errorhandler, before_request, and friends) that both the application object and its modular sub-parts (blueprints) share. It also knows how to start a simple development web server, sets up a default logger, and produces extra-friendly error messages in debug mode for common mistakes. In short, this is the object that turns a collection of Python functions into a runnable website.

units.name: blueprints
units.role: Reusable, prefixable bundles of routes and handlers that can be registered onto an application.
units.description: This unit implements Flask's Blueprint feature: a way to define a reusable, self-contained bundle of routes, view functions, error handlers, and template helpers that can later be registered onto a real application, optionally under a URL prefix or subdomain, and even nested inside other blueprints. It lets large web applications be split into independently authored, pluggable pieces that only become live once registered with the app.

units.name: request-context
units.role: Per-request/app-context local storage and the current_app/g/request/session proxy objects.
units.description: This unit implements Flask's 'current context' mechanism: the storage that lets any piece of code, anywhere in a request handler or CLI command, ask 'which app and which incoming request am I running for right now?' without that information being explicitly passed as a function argument. It defines the context object that is created and pushed when a request or CLI invocation begins, holding the active app, the incoming request, the session, and a scratch space for the duration of that request, and it is popped and cleaned up when the request ends. It also defines the four proxy objects (current_app, g, request, session) that code imports and uses as if they were simple globals, even though they always resolve to whichever request is currently being handled.

units.name: http-wrappers
units.role: Flask's Request and Response classes, extending Werkzeug's with Flask-specific conveniences.
units.description: This unit defines Flask's own versions of an HTTP 'request' (the incoming data from a browser or API client) and 'response' (what gets sent back). They are built on top of a lower-level library (Werkzeug) but add Flask-specific conveniences, such as knowing which URL rule and blueprint matched a request, honoring the app's configured size limits, and plugging in Flask's JSON handling. Every request a Flask app handles and every response it sends passes through these two classes.

entrypoints.name: Request
entrypoints.plain: Represents one incoming HTTP request, with Flask-specific extras layered on Werkzeug's request object.

entrypoints.name: Response
entrypoints.plain: Represents the HTTP response Flask sends back, with Flask-specific extras layered on Werkzeug's response object.

units.name: json-serialization
units.role: Converts Python values to/from JSON for HTTP responses, and provides the tagged-JSON format used by session cookies.
units.description: This code turns Python values (dicts, lists, dates, UUIDs, bytes, and similar) into JSON text for HTTP responses and back again when reading requests. It gives every Flask app a default set of JSON rules via jsonify/dumps/loads/dump/load, which apps can swap out for a different JSON library by replacing the pluggable JSON provider. It also includes a special compact 'tagged JSON' format used only for the secure session cookie, which can round-trip Python types that plain JSON does not support (like datetimes, UUIDs, and raw bytes) while keeping the encoded cookie small.

units.name: sessions
units.role: Reads and writes the signed cookie that stores a visitor's session data across requests.
units.description: This unit defines how Flask remembers information about a visitor between separate web requests (their session), such as being logged in. It defines the shape of a session object and the default mechanism for storing it: packing the session's contents into JSON, cryptographically signing the result so it cannot be tampered with, and storing it in a browser cookie. On each incoming request it verifies and unpacks the cookie back into the session dictionary, and on each outgoing response it re-signs and re-writes the cookie (or deletes it) if the session changed.

units.name: config
units.role: Loads application settings from Python files/objects, JSON/TOML files, or environment variables into one dict-like object.
units.description: This unit defines how a Flask application's settings (things like SECRET_KEY, DEBUG mode, database URLs, etc.) are stored and loaded. It provides a dictionary-like object that application authors fill in one of several ways: writing values directly, pointing at a Python file, pointing at a Python module or class, pointing at a JSON/TOML file, or reading environment variables, including an auto-prefixed convention like FLASK_SOME_KEY. Once populated, the rest of the framework and the developer's own code read settings out of this single object.

units.name: templating
units.role: Sets up Jinja2 across the app and its blueprints, and renders templates to strings or streams.
units.description: This part of Flask lets a web application define HTML (or other text) templates and fill them in with live data to produce the final page a user sees. It knows how to find template files not just in the main application's folder but also in the folders of any registered blueprints, so templates can be organized modularly. It offers both a normal render (get back a complete string) and a streaming render (send the page to the browser piece by piece as it's generated), and it notifies other parts of the application when a template is about to be, and has been, rendered.

units.name: request-helpers
units.role: Utility functions view code calls directly: url_for, redirect, abort, flash, send_file, and related helpers.
units.description: This file provides the small toolbox of functions a Flask application's view code calls directly while handling a web request: building a URL for another route, sending the browser to a different page, stopping and returning an HTTP error, queuing a one-time notice for the user to see on their next page load, serving a file or a directory of files from disk, pulling a value out of a template, wrapping up a return value into a proper response, and keeping request data available while streaming a long response. It also holds a few lower-level utilities the framework itself uses at startup, such as reading debug-mode environment variables and finding a package's folder on disk.

units.name: cli
units.role: The `flask` command-line tool: dev server, shell, routes listing, app discovery, and .env loading.
units.description: This is the flask command-line tool. It lets a developer type commands like 'flask run' to start a local development server, 'flask shell' to open an interactive Python session with their app already loaded, and 'flask routes' to list the URLs their app responds to. It also knows how to find the developer's application, from the FLASK_APP environment variable, a command-line option, or by guessing common file names, and how to read configuration secrets from .env and .flaskenv files before the app starts.

units.name: class-based-views
units.role: Lets developers define view handlers as classes (View, MethodView) instead of plain functions.
units.description: This code provides an alternative, object-oriented way for developers to write the functions that handle web requests in a Flask application. Instead of writing a single plain function for a URL, a developer can write a class with methods like get() and post() for each HTTP verb, and reuse setup logic across them. A helper called as_view() takes such a class and wraps it into the ordinary function-shaped object that Flask's URL routing system knows how to call, so class-based views can be registered exactly like regular view functions.

units.name: signals
units.role: Named lifecycle events other code can subscribe to, backed by the blinker library.
units.description: This unit defines a set of named signals that Flask announces at key moments while it handles a web request: when a request starts, when it finishes, when an error occurs, when a template is about to render or has rendered, when the application context is pushed or popped, and when a flash message is queued. Other code, whether inside Flask or written by someone using Flask, can subscribe to these announcements and run its own logic in response, without having to change Flask's own code.

violations_observed.location: src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:119 (class Blueprint(Scaffold)), and its use of app.error_handler_spec/before_request_funcs/after_request_funcs/view_functions/template_context_processors/url_value_preprocessors/url_default_functions in Blueprint.register/_merge_blueprint_funcs
violations_observed.note: Blueprint subclasses application-core's Scaffold directly, inheriting its route/error-handler/before-after-teardown decorator methods verbatim rather than calling them as an external API, and Blueprint.register reads and writes Scaffold's internal attribute dictionaries on the app object directly. This is a shared-base-class/shared-data-model coupling, not a call to a listed entrypoint, so the depends_on edge to 'Scaffold' only approximates the real coupling.

debughelpers.py, part of application-core, imports Blueprint from the blueprints unit purely to isinstance()-check it inside explain_template_loading_attempts for a nicer diagnostic label. Combined with blueprints depending on application-core's Scaffold, the two units are mutually coupled rather than having a one-directional dependency.

add_url_rule reads getattr(view_func, "methods", None) and getattr(view_func, "provide_automatic_options", None) — attributes that View.as_view() attaches to the generated view function. This is a duck-typed contract between the two units, not a call to a class-based-views entrypoint, so it is not expressed as a depends_on edge.
